evidence.supports: Museum's own first-edition record identifies Jane Austen as writer, T. Egerton as publisher, January 1813 as publication, one novel issued in three volumes, the 1796 First Impressions draft and substantial 1811–1812 revision.
Folger's collection record identifies the 1813 first edition, October 1796–August 1797 early writing period, and Elizabeth Bennet as a fictional heroine of similar age to the young Austen.
British Library classic list pairs Pride and Prejudice with Austen; the three distractors are paired with different novels: Shelley/Frankenstein, Brontë/Jane Eyre, Eliot/Middlemarch.

items.review_note: The article distinguishes draft, revision and first publication; writer, publisher and fictional character; and proposes a conditional bibliographic comparison without claiming a single literary interpretation. No physical-object inspection or exact-day/print-run claim is made.

evidence.supports: Presidential Library's Dostoevsky section identifies the novel and 1866 Russkii vestnik journal installments; the issue bibliography says edition of M. Katkov. General contributor names on the catalogue page are not treated as coauthors.

Displayed modern digital reprint identifies Dostoevsky and six parts plus epilogue. Its opening directly supports July heat, cramped lodging, anxiety about the landlady, Petersburg streets, and Raskolnikov's name in dialogue.

University of Toronto Libraries exhibition independently credits Dostoevsky and distinguishes the 1866 journal appearance from a 1867 separate edition; it attributes War and Peace to Tolstoy and Fathers and Sons to Turgenev.
Library of Congress NLS collection note identifies Dead Souls as Gogol's work, accounting for the fourth option.

items.review_note: The article describes only the 1866 journal context and the displayed beginning of a modern digital reprint. It does not date all separate book editions, conflate Raskolnikov with Dostoevsky, infer diagnosis or sole motive, or present one compulsory interpretation.
